input.question: Beyond individual preference or taste, what determines whether unrelated flavor pairings are amazing or absolutely gross?
input.ground_truth: All foods contain flavor compounds. For example, the aroma of banana and pear is a compound called isoamyl acetate. Flavor pairing is simply matching foods together that have the same flavor compounds. Want to know what foods match together? Over the last 5 years the website _URL_1_(requires creating an account) has been steadily identifying the compounds in over 1000 different vegetables, prepared meats, spices, juices, flowers, etc. into their pairing database. Question: Beyond individual preference or taste, what determines whether unrelated flavor pairings are amazing or absolutely gross?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have two toys: one is sweet like candy, and the other is sour like a lemon. When you put them together, sometimes they make a fun surprise, like a sweet and sour candy that tastes really good. But sometimes, if you mix two toys that are both super sour, or both super spicy, it might make your mouth feel weird or yucky.

So, when grown-ups (or chefs) put together foods that don’t usually go together, like chocolate and broccoli, it can taste funny or even bad to us. That’s because our tongue and brain have special sensors that like some mixes and don’t like others. Also, our brains remember what we’ve eaten before and what feels normal. If something is too weird or too much, our brain says, “Yuck!” But if it’s just right, our brain says, “Wow, that’s cool!”

So, it’s like playing with toys: some combinations are fun and some aren’t, and everyone has their own favorite ways to play!
